RECOMMENDATION: Standard clopidogrel dosing per prescribing information. Enhanced platelet inhibition possible — monitor for bleeding, particularly in patients with high bleeding risk.
Standard clopidogrel dosing per prescribing information.
Consider alternative antiplatelet therapy (e.g., prasugrel or ticagrelor) if clinically feasible. If clopidogrel is used, be aware of reduced efficacy; platelet function testing may be warranted.

Use alternative antiplatelet therapy (prasugrel or ticagrelor). Clopidogrel is essentially contraindicated — absent CYP2C19 activity prevents formation of the active thiol metabolite. Do not use clopidogrel in ACS or PCI settings.

Increased dose may be required for H. pylori eradication (use 40 mg BID) or severe erosive oesophagitis. Consider alternative PPI with less CYP2C19 dependence (e.g., rabeprazole or pantoprazole) for long-term use.
Standard omeprazole dosing per prescribing information.
Standard omeprazole dose is appropriate. Slightly increased exposure may improve acid suppression in GERD — no dose adjustment required.

Initiate at 50% of standard dose. Poor metabolizers have 5-10x higher omeprazole AUC; significantly increased risk of adverse effects (headache, diarrhoea, elevated liver enzymes). Titrate cautiously.

Avoid voriconazole if clinically feasible — subtherapeutic plasma levels are likely at standard dosing due to ultra-rapid clearance. Use alternative antifungal (e.g., isavuconazole, liposomal amphotericin B, or echinocandin). If no alternative, use therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with significantly increased dose.
Standard voriconazole dosing per prescribing information. TDM recommended for critically ill patients.
Initiate standard voriconazole dose. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is recommended — higher target trough concentrations (2-5.5 mg/L) are typical in this group.

Avoid voriconazole if clinically feasible. Poor metabolizers have 4-fold higher AUC than Normal Metabolizers; high risk of neurotoxicity and hepatotoxicity. If unavoidable, initiate at 50% standard dose with intensive TDM (target trough 1-5.5 mg/L) and liver function monitoring.
Standard warfarin dosing per prescribing information. Initiate per clinical algorithm (e.g., Warfarin Dosing Service or Gage algorithm). Standard INR monitoring schedule.

Reduce initial warfarin dose by 25%. Increased warfarin sensitivity — time to stable INR is prolonged. Increase INR monitoring frequency for first 4 weeks. Target INR remains 2.0-3.0 for most indications.

Reduce initial warfarin dose by 50% or more. Severely impaired warfarin clearance — bleeding risk is substantially elevated. Weekly INR monitoring required for a minimum of 4 weeks. Consider bridging anticoagulation and haematology/pharmacy consultation.
Standard ibuprofen dosing per prescribing information. No pharmacogenomic action required.
Use ibuprofen with caution; initiate at lowest effective dose and shortest duration. Moderately reduced clearance leads to elevated plasma exposure; GI and renal toxicity risk is modestly increased.

Initiate at lowest effective dose with shortest duration possible. Significantly reduced clearance — NSAID-related GI bleeding, renal impairment, and cardiovascular events are elevated risks. Consider alternative analgesic (paracetamol, topical NSAID) where feasible.

Avoid codeine — risk of life-threatening opioid toxicity. Ultra-rapid conversion to morphine produces plasma morphine concentrations 50% higher than Normal Metabolizers. Fatalities reported, especially in children, breastfed infants, and post-tonsillectomy patients. Use alternative analgesic (e.g., non-opioid, or morphine/oxycodone at standard doses).
Standard codeine dosing per prescribing information.
Use codeine with caution; reduced analgesia is expected due to lower morphine production. If pain control is inadequate, consider alternative analgesic rather than increasing codeine dose.

Avoid codeine — ineffective analgesia. Negligible conversion to the active morphine metabolite. No therapeutic benefit; use alternative analgesic (non-opioid preferred, or alternative opioid such as morphine or oxycodone).

Avoid amitriptyline or use substantially higher dose with therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM). Standard doses likely to produce subtherapeutic plasma levels; poor antidepressant response expected. If TCA is required, choose nortriptyline or imipramine with close monitoring.
Standard amitriptyline dosing per prescribing information. TDM at steady state is advisable for all TCAs.
Initiate amitriptyline at 25% lower dose and titrate according to clinical response and TDM. Moderately increased drug exposure — monitor for anticholinergic and cardiac adverse effects.

Avoid amitriptyline — 2-fold increase in exposure at standard doses; high risk of anticholinergic toxicity (QTc prolongation, urinary retention, confusion) and serotonergic adverse effects. If TCA is required, use nortriptyline or desipramine at 50% starting dose with TDM.
Standard efavirenz 600 mg/day per WHO and prescribing information. No pharmacogenomic dose adjustment required.
Standard efavirenz 600 mg/day. Monitor for CNS adverse effects (vivid dreams, dizziness, depression) which are more common in this group. TDM recommended if adverse effects arise.

Reduce efavirenz to 400 mg/day (from standard 600 mg/day). Poor metabolizers have markedly elevated efavirenz plasma levels — increased CNS toxicity (severe neuropsychiatric effects, suicidality) and treatment discontinuation rates. Consult HIV pharmacist; 400 mg/day has demonstrated non-inferior virological efficacy in ENCORE1 trial (PMID:24411081).
Standard methadone initiation per prescribing information. Low starting dose with gradual titration; close monitoring for the first 2 weeks.
Standard methadone initiation with careful monitoring. Slightly elevated methadone exposure — monitor ECG (QTc) and respiratory rate during titration.

Initiate methadone at lowest possible dose with very slow titration (no more than 5 mg increases every 7 days). Reduced clearance increases accumulation risk — respiratory depression and QTc prolongation are elevated risks. Consider alternative opioid agonist therapy (e.g., buprenorphine) if available.
Standard simvastatin dosing per prescribing information. No dose adjustment for pharmacogenomic reasons.

Use simvastatin ≤20 mg/day or switch to an alternative statin with lower SLCO1B1 sensitivity: pravastatin (40-80 mg/day), rosuvastatin (10-20 mg/day), or fluvastatin XL (80 mg/day). Risk of simvastatin-induced myopathy is 2-4 fold elevated. If higher-intensity statin therapy is needed, rosuvastatin is preferred.

Avoid simvastatin entirely. Risk of severe myopathy/rhabdomyolysis is ~17-fold elevated vs normal function. Use pravastatin, rosuvastatin, or fluvastatin — these have minimal SLCO1B1 dependence. Atorvastatin is intermediate risk and may be used with caution at lower doses.
Standard atorvastatin dosing per prescribing information.
Standard atorvastatin dosing is acceptable; myopathy risk is modestly elevated compared to simvastatin. Avoid doses >40 mg/day if possible. Monitor for muscle symptoms (myalgia, elevated CK).

Use atorvastatin with caution at lowest effective dose (≤20 mg/day); monitor CK and muscle symptoms. If higher-intensity LDL lowering is required, consider rosuvastatin or pravastatin as lower-risk alternatives.
Standard azathioprine dosing per prescribing information (typically 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/day for autoimmune conditions). Routine CBC monitoring per standard protocol.

Reduce azathioprine starting dose to 30-70% of standard dose. Allow 2-4 weeks between dose adjustments. Increase CBC monitoring frequency (every 2 weeks for first 2 months). Full therapeutic effect is achievable at reduced doses.

Avoid azathioprine — risk of severe, potentially fatal thiopurine toxicity (myelosuppression, neutropenia, infections). Use alternative non-thiopurine immunosuppressant (e.g., mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, cyclosporine depending on indication). If thiopurine is absolutely required, use 10% of standard dose with very frequent CBC monitoring under specialist supervision.
Standard 6-mercaptopurine dosing per prescribing information. Routine haematological monitoring per oncology/gastroenterology protocol.
Reduce starting 6-MP dose to 30-70% of standard dose. Start at 50% and titrate based on haematological response and tolerability. CBC monitoring every 2 weeks for first 2 months.
Reduce starting 6-MP dose to 10% of standard dose. Begin at 10% and titrate slowly. Weekly CBC monitoring for the first 8 weeks minimum. Consider haematology/clinical pharmacology consultation.
Standard 6-mercaptopurine dosing per prescribing information.
Reduce starting 6-MP dose by 30-50%. Increase frequency of CBC monitoring. Titrate dose based on tolerability and haematological response.

Reduce starting 6-MP dose to 10% of standard dose. Risk of severe myelosuppression is very high — especially critical in paediatric ALL patients. Weekly CBC monitoring. Consider haematology consultation before initiation.
Standard azathioprine dosing per prescribing information.
Reduce azathioprine starting dose by 30-50%. Monitor CBC closely every 2 weeks for first 2 months.
Reduce azathioprine starting dose to 10% of standard dose or use alternative immunosuppressant. Very high myelosuppression risk. Frequent CBC monitoring mandatory.
